blocks.p: Appease and fawn are often called mixed states. When two (or all) primary states are active simultaneously, they create a mixed state.

Appeasement is conceptualized as a co-regulatory mixed state. Appease emerges in scenarios of extreme life-threat, such as a hostage situation. It's positioned as a "super social engagement," where the individual utilizes social interaction skills even under intense threat. It's even suggested that appeasement should replace the concept of "Stockholm Syndrome."

This mixed state combines all three of the primary states as a defensive measure. The safety state is still accessible to the individual in a captive life-threat scenario. They use their "super social engagement" to send cues of safety to the perpetrator. This may serve to calm the perpetrator enough to stay alive. This may have served an evolutionary purpose. Since "... in early civilization, there was always a risk of being captured or killed by another social group. Bonding with captors increased the chance of survival."

The captive aligns with the perpetrator in their goals and means, including against authorities. The appeaser develops positive feelings for their captor, possibly even gratitude for sparing their life. They identify the captor's happiness and well-being as directly linked to their own: "I'm on your team and not a threat. I can help you. You can trust me."

None of this is chosen. The nervous system adapts based on the needs of survival. In these extreme captive situations, the victim is entirely reliant upon the captor for their basic needs. The ability to connect and appease a danger could result in living for another day and the possibility of escape.

From the viewpoint of the Polyvagal Theory, fawn is a combination of sympathetic and dorsal vagal activation. It occurs in scenarios of ongoing, inescapable, and unrelenting life threats, like abusive homes. Fawn is similar to appeasement but distinct.

The individual using fawn is not sending safety cues, like appeasement. Instead, they placate the life-threat through compliance. Fawning reduces threat by tending to the needs and wants of the abuser. The person in fawn wants to be invisible and hide: "I'm not a problem, and there's nothing to worry about. Please don't get upset."

The fawner quietly attempts to please the abuser by creating and extending periods of de-escalation. They preemptively anticipate and fulfill the abuser's needs. The fawner sacrifices their values and agency in the hope that the abuser will lose interest.

It's very dangerous for mammals to enter shutdown. We evolved to enter and exit it fairly quickly. In shutdown, there is a major reduction in breathing (apnea) and heart rate (bradycardia). But mammals require lots and lots of oxygen for their big brains. So, the ability to sustain life in this state is not good, to put it very simply.

What happens when someone is stuck in a chronically life-threatening situation? When they can't run, can't fight back, and can't exist in shutdown for very long? Instead of collapsing in a complete shutdown and risking death, the individual will enter into a chronic state of dissociation. They will disconnect from their reality and themself. This permits the individual to continue functioning and stay alive.

In my opinion, but not explicitly discussed in primary source Polyvagal writings as of early 2024, both fawn and appeasement must require significant dissociation. I won't go into details, but appeasement and fawn can lead to behaviors that seriously violate the appeaser's and fawner's values. They may lead to violating innocent people, covering up immoral/illegal acts, deceiving authorities, and otherwise assisting the abuser/captor with their immoral/illegal deeds.

Both fawning and appeasing must require the individual to disconnect from their values, social norms, internal empathy and compassion, and sympathetic flight/fight empowerment. If this is true, then the individual must exist in a dominant dorsal vagal shutdown state through the lens of the Polyvagal Theory. Dominant shutdown leads to numbness, emptiness, dissociation, and decreased cognitive functioning.

There are also potentially less extreme versions of appease and fawn that don't require dissociation. You may have seen a dog tensely roll over and lick a dominant pack leader. The dog is immobile but mobilized (tense and rolled over) while also socially engaging (lick). This would be an example of appeasement. People liken "people pleasing" as a common everyday form of fawning.

I personally don't give much time or attention to appease and fawn. I conceptualize them more as behavioral adaptations than Polyvagal states. This is a much bigger conversation. If you're interested, listen to episode 204 of my Stuck Not Broken podcast, or read [why fawning isn't a survival state](piece:fawn-response).

blocks.prompt: What is the one state you spend the most amount of time in currently?
What is the one state you spent the most amount of time in when you were a young child? An adolescent? How about as you've aged?
What state(s) did you spend less time in?
What state(s) would you like to spend more time in?
Did you choose to spend more or less time in these states? Or was it a result of context?

q: "We operationally define this capacity to co-regulate and calm the perpetrator as appeasement. The ability to access the appeasement process is conceptualised as a type of 'super social engagement' that requires the neural capacity to manage a hybrid state that enables access to the calming and social cuing of the social engagement system (Porges, 2011, 2021, 2022), while simultaneously maintaining access to the energetic mobilisation sympathetic system to engage fight/flight behaviours if necessary (Porges, 2011). Firsthand accounts from survivors of abduction underscore their awareness of the importance of establishing some type of social connection with the perpetrator." (Bailey et al)
blocks.cite: Bailey, R., Dugard, J., Smith, S. F., & Porges, S. W. (2023). Appeasement: Replacing Stockholm syndrome as a definition of a survival strategy. European Journal of Psychotraumatology, 14(1), 2161038. [doi.org/10.1080/20008066.2022.2161038](https://doi.org/10.1080/20008066.2022.2161038)

blocks.p: My translation: Calming a threatening person is called "appeasement." It involves using our ability to socially engage when ready to fight or run if needed.

q: "Activating the neural substrate to appease is a challenge to the nervous system and is not an easily accessible intentional behaviour. Rather, it requires a retuning of the autonomic state that opportunistically maintains sufficient inhibition over the adaptive threat reactions of the sympathetic nervous system (i.e. fight/flight) or the dorsal vagal system (i.e. shutdown, collapse, fainting, defecation). By placing an autonomic state at the core of feelings of safety or threat, the pragmatic survival behaviours of fight and flight and complex problem-solving strategies that would lead to escape are consequential and dependent on the facilitatory function of the autonomic nervous system in optimising these strategies...." (Bailey et al)
blocks.cite: Bailey, R., Dugard, J., Smith, S. F., & Porges, S. W. (2023). Appeasement: Replacing Stockholm syndrome as a definition of a survival strategy. European Journal of Psychotraumatology, 14(1), 2161038. [doi.org/10.1080/20008066.2022.2161038](https://doi.org/10.1080/20008066.2022.2161038)

blocks.p: My translation: Appeasement is hard and not a choice. The body needs a balance between calm and readiness to fight or flee. The strength of your safety state is important in tolerating defensive activation.

q: "When faced with a threat, we sometimes fight or flee. Other times we freeze or shut down. But for some of us, the nervous system tries to navigate the treacherous journey from danger to safety with yet another strategy: an attempt to support, and even soothe, a perpetrator who means us harm. These responses are most common when somebody is surrounded by a pervasive and nearly nonstop threat, as is the case with those who have been abducted or who live in a chronically abusive environment." (Porges & Porges)
blocks.cite: Porges, S. W., & Porges, S. (2023). Our Polyvagal World: How Safety and Trauma Change Us. W. W. Norton & Company.
